content: The data provided outlines findings related to the use of dolutegravir (DTG) during pregnancy and its potential effects on maternal and neonatal outcomes, as well as congenital anomalies. Below is a professional interpretation of the information: 1. Maternal Outcomes and Viral Load Reduction: Among 90 women with baseline RNA levels permitting a 1-log reduction, the median time to achieve this reduction was significantly shorter in the group receiving integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) compared to the non-INSTI group (8 days vs. 35 days, respectively). A restricted sub-analysis showed similar results (7 days for INSTI vs. 11 days for non-INSTI). All women receiving dolutegravir (DTG) achieved a greater than 1-log reduction in viral load. 2. Pregnancy Outcomes: Preterm delivery (<37 weeks) and very preterm delivery (<32 weeks) were reported. Small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants (<10th percentile) occurred in 25% of DTG-exposed pregnancies, with very SGA (<3rd percentile) also noted. Low birth weight (<2500 g) and very low birth weight (<1500 g) were observed, along with stillbirths and miscarriages. However, all live-born children were uninfected with HIV. 3. Pharmacokinetics of DTG in Pregnancy: At 35 weeks of gestation, maternal steady-state total and unbound DTG concentrations were 3007 ng/mL and 44 ng/mL, respectively. Neonatal DTG levels decreased over time, with complete elimination by day 18 of life. The terminal half-life of DTG was prolonged in preterm infants compared to adults, suggesting potential accumulation in the fetal compartment due to placental transfer and slower neonatal clearance. Co-administration of atazanavir (ATV) may have contributed to this effect by inhibiting DTG metabolism. 4. Congenital Anomalies: Congenital anomalies were reported across various organ systems, including: Central Nervous System (CNS): Cardiac Defects: These included ventricular septal defects (VSD), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and anomalous pulmonary venous connections. Renal Anomalies: Ectopic kidneys, renal hypoplasia, congenital hydronephrosis, and renal cysts were among the reported defects. Musculoskeletal Defects: Polydactyly and syndactyly were observed. Genetic Abnormalities: Cases of Down syndrome and other genetic mutations were reported. Other Anomalies: Esophageal atresia, facial dysmorphia, and intracranial calcifications were noted. 5. Trimester-Specific Findings: 6. Pharmacovigilance Data: Congenital anomalies were reported in 1.4% of pregnancies, with neural tube defects being a key concern. Cardiac, renal, and musculoskeletal anomalies were also documented. 7. WHO Data on DTG and Triumeq: Data from the WHO VigiAccess system included 2095 records for DTG alone and 2237 records for Triumeq (DTG/ABC/3TC). Congenital anomalies were reported in both groups, with cardiac and renal defects being the most common. No CNS defects were reported in these datasets. These findings underscore the importance of careful monitoring and counseling for women of childbearing potential who are prescribed DTG.
